explain.say: Here is a puzzle. Breaking big atoms apart gives out energy. But sticking tiny atoms together also gives out energy. How can both be true? Let us put the two side by side: fission and fusion.

explain.say: Fission, yes! It does leave radioactive waste that must be stored safely for a very long time. Now the right card: fusion. Two tiny nuclei, like hydrogen, crash together and join to make helium. Which one joins things?

explain.say: Fusion, right! It powers the Sun and every star. But nuclei repel each other, so they must smash together incredibly fast. That needs temperatures of millions of degrees, so it is very hard to do on Earth. Why do you think it needs so much heat?

explain.say: To make the nuclei fast enough to join, brilliant! In both cases, a little mass turns into a lot of energy. Wow fact: the Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second. Scientists at ITER in France are building a fusion machine to copy it. Challenge: which is cleaner, and why?

faq.q: What is the difference between fission and fusion?
faq.a: Fission splits a large nucleus into smaller ones. Fusion joins small nuclei into a larger one. Both release energy.

faq.q: Why is fusion so hard to do on Earth?
faq.a: Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so they must be heated to over 100 million degrees to collide hard enough to fuse.
asks: Why don't we have fusion power yet?

faq.q: How does the Sun make energy?
faq.a: In its core, at about 15 million degrees, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing huge amounts of energy.

faq.q: Where does the energy come from in both reactions?
faq.a: In both, the products have a little less mass than the starting nuclei. That mass is turned into energy.
asks: Why do fission and fusion release energy?

faq.q: Which is cleaner, fission or fusion?
faq.a: Fusion would produce far less long-lived radioactive waste, and its fuel comes from water, but it is not yet a working power source.

facts: The Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second.
The core of the Sun is about 15 million °C; fusion reactors on Earth need over 100 million °C.

quiz.why: In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium.

wrong.1: Fission splits heavy nuclei; the Sun joins light ones.
wrong.2: The Sun is not a chemical fire; it is nuclear.

quiz.why: Fission is the splitting of a large nucleus like uranium-235.

wrong.2: Fission needs fuel such as uranium.
